cemc-galois-2005-01a.prompt:
An *arithmetic sequence* is a sequence in which each term after the first is obtained from the previous term by adding a constant. For example, the sequence $2, 11, 20, 29, \dots$ is an arithmetic sequence. (The "$\dots$" indicates that this sequence continues without ever ending.)

Find the $11$th term in the arithmetic sequence $17, 22, 27, 32, \dots$.

cemc-galois-2005-01b.prompt:
An *arithmetic sequence* is a sequence in which each term after the first is obtained from the previous term by adding a constant. For example, the sequence $2, 11, 20, 29, \dots$ is an arithmetic sequence. (The "$\dots$" indicates that this sequence continues without ever ending.)

Explain why there is no number which occurs in each of the following arithmetic sequences:
$$17, 22, 27, 32, \dots \qquad 13, 28, 43, 58, \dots$$
cemc-galois-2005-01b.answer: Terms of the first end in $7$ or $2$; terms of the second end in $3$ or $8$. (Equivalently $17 + 5n = 13 + 15m$ gives $4 = 5(3m - n)$, impossible.)

cemc-galois-2005-02a.prompt:
Emilia and Omar are playing a game in which they take turns placing numbered tiles on a grid with $3$ rows and $4$ columns. Emilia starts the game with six tiles: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$. Omar also starts the game with six tiles: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$. Once a tile is placed, it cannot be moved.

After all of the tiles have been placed, Emilia scores one point for each row that has an even sum and one point for each column that has an even sum. Omar scores one point for each row that has an odd sum and one point for each column that has an odd sum. For example, if the game ends with the tiles placed as shown below, then Emilia will score $5$ points and Omar $2$ points.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 5 | 5 | 2 | 4 |
| 1 | 3 | 6 | 6 |

In a game, after Omar has placed his second last tile, the grid appears as shown below. Starting with the partially completed game shown, give a final placement of tiles for which Omar scores more points than Emilia. (You do not have to give a strategy, simply fill in the final grid.)

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | | 5 |
| 3 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| | 4 | 4 | |
cemc-galois-2005-02a.answer: Top row: $1, 3, 6, 5$; bottom row: $5, 4, 4, 6$. Column sums $9, 8, 12, 13$ and row sums $15, 8, 19$: Omar $4$, Emilia $3$.

cemc-galois-2005-02b.prompt:
Emilia and Omar are playing a game in which they take turns placing numbered tiles on a grid with $3$ rows and $4$ columns. Emilia starts the game with six tiles: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$. Omar also starts the game with six tiles: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$. Once a tile is placed, it cannot be moved.

After all of the tiles have been placed, Emilia scores one point for each row that has an even sum and one point for each column that has an even sum. Omar scores one point for each row that has an odd sum and one point for each column that has an odd sum. For example, if the game ends with the tiles placed as shown below, then Emilia will score $5$ points and Omar $2$ points.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 5 | 5 | 2 | 4 |
| 1 | 3 | 6 | 6 |

Explain why it is impossible for Omar and Emilia to score the same number of points in any game.
cemc-galois-2005-02b.answer: There are $3 + 4 = 7$ lines, each giving exactly one point to one player; $7$ is odd, so the scores can't be equal.

cemc-galois-2005-02c.prompt:
Emilia and Omar are playing a game in which they take turns placing numbered tiles on a grid with $3$ rows and $4$ columns. Emilia starts the game with six tiles: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$. Omar also starts the game with six tiles: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$. Once a tile is placed, it cannot be moved.

After all of the tiles have been placed, Emilia scores one point for each row that has an even sum and one point for each column that has an even sum. Omar scores one point for each row that has an odd sum and one point for each column that has an odd sum. For example, if the game ends with the tiles placed as shown below, then Emilia will score $5$ points and Omar $2$ points.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 5 | 5 | 2 | 4 |
| 1 | 3 | 6 | 6 |

In the partially completed game shown below, it is Omar's turn to play and he has a $2$ and a $5$ still to place. Explain why Omar cannot score more points than Emilia, no matter where he places the $5$.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | 3 | 6 |
| | 5 | | 4 |
| 3 | | 1 | 6 |
cemc-galois-2005-02c.answer: Remaining tiles are $2, 2, 4, 5$ (one odd). Column 4 is even ($16$); rows 1 and 3 and columns 1 and 3 each have one gap and an even sum so far, and the single odd tile can make at most one of them odd. So Emilia gets at least $1 + 3 = 4$ of $7$ points.

cemc-galois-2005-03a.prompt:
Two identical rectangular crates are packed with cylindrical pipes, using different methods. Each pipe has diameter $10$ cm. A side view of the first four rows of each of the two different methods of packing is shown: in Crate A every row has $10$ pipes stacked directly on top of the row below; in Crate B the rows alternate between $10$ and $9$ pipes, each pipe resting in the gap between two pipes of the row below.

If $200$ pipes are packed in each of the two crates, how many rows of pipes are there in each crate? Explain your answer.
cemc-galois-2005-03a.answer: Crate A: $20$ rows; Crate B: $21$ rows.

cemc-galois-2005-04a.prompt:
The volume of a sphere with radius $r$ is $\frac43 \pi r^3$. The *total* surface area of a cone with height $h$, slant height $s$, and radius $r$ is $\pi r^2 + \pi r s$.

A cylinder has a height of $10$ and a radius of $3$. Determine the *total* surface area, including the two ends, of the cylinder, and also determine the volume of the cylinder.

cemc-galois-2005-04b.prompt:
The volume of a sphere with radius $r$ is $\frac43 \pi r^3$. The *total* surface area of a cone with height $h$, slant height $s$, and radius $r$ is $\pi r^2 + \pi r s$.

A cone, a cylinder and a sphere all have radius $r$. The height of the cylinder is $H$ and the height of the cone is $h$. The cylinder and the sphere have the same volume. The cone and the cylinder have the same total surface area. Prove that $h$ and $H$ cannot both be integers.
cemc-galois-2005-04b.answer: Volumes give $H = \frac43 r$; surface areas give $s = r + 2H$; with $s = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$ this leads to $h^2 = 7H^2$, so $h = \sqrt7\,H$, and $\sqrt7$ is irrational.
